title: Breath poured as an offering
hookLine: in the Gita's list of offerings, some people offer their breath, and it sits in a row with everyone else's gift
carry: even a breath can be yajna, an offering
tomorrow: breath is Brahman, so why keep looking?

cards: What would it mean to give a breath away? Not to hold it, or push it, or count it. To offer it, the way a person sets a flower down in front of an image or pours a spoon of ghee into a fire.

In the fourth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna walks Arjuna through a long list of offerings people make. Wealth, study, discipline, the restraint of the senses. And in the middle of the list, quietly, breath.
Today: what the Gita does with the breath, and the verse that turns a family dinner into an offering.

teach.b: Here's the verse, in paraphrase. Some, Krishna says, offer the in-breath into the out-breath, and the out-breath into the in-breath, holding the path of both, given over to the practice of breath.
The breath going in is poured into the breath going out, like ghee into a fire, and back again. Breathing itself becomes a yajna, a sacrifice.
That's the teaching: in the Gita, any act can be an offering, not only what's poured into a temple fire. Look at the company breath keeps. Some offer their senses into the fire of restraint.
Some offer their possessions. Some offer austerity, some study, some yoga. And a short line sums up the row: all of these know what sacrifice is.
You'll sometimes hear that the Gita crowns breath control as the highest yoga. It doesn't. Breath gets its own careful verse, in a row of gifts.
The point isn't what you get from the breath, but what you give with it. A few verses earlier sits the line that makes this a daily habit.
In paraphrase: the offering is Brahman, the ghee is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman.

teach.h: YAJNA: ANY ACT CAN BE AN OFFERING
teach.b: Many Hindus chant that verse before eating, so the plate becomes an offering and the meal a small yajna.
In the fifth chapter, the Gita mentions evening out the in-breath and out-breath within the nostrils, and there too breath serves a larger aim: a person free of desire, fear and anger.

teach.h: NOT WHAT YOU GET, BUT WHAT YOU GIVE
teach.b: Eating, breathing, the most ordinary things, can be given.

how: Many Hindus chant Gita 4.24 ('the offering is Brahman…') before meals, and some treat daily actions, breathing among them, as offerings in the spirit of the Gita's fourth chapter.

o: a breath held as long as you can before a fire
a secret breath kept only for the highest yogis
breath as an offering, one gift in a row of gifts

games.q: the row of offerings — tap the pairs.

s: the Gita's fourth chapter crowns breath control as the highest yoga
breath stands in a row with study, giving and restraint. the list doesn't crown it.
in the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath
breathing becomes an offering, poured back and forth like a gift into a fire.
many Hindus chant a Gita verse before eating
'the offering is Brahman', from chapter four, so the meal becomes an offering too.

games.q: you're Krishna, listing the ways people make offerings. where does breath go?
o: at the top, above everything else.
left out: it's only the body.
in the row, alongside study, giving and restraint.
games.why: breath gets its own careful verse, in the middle of the list, and the Gita says all of these know what sacrifice is.

practice: Notice the breath in arriving and let it flow into the breath out without a seam, then the breath out turning into the breath in, like the gentlest offering: something set down, not thrown.
If you pray, you can offer your breathing, just as it is, to God, as some Hindus do; if you don't, you can simply let it go with thanks.

wordCard.voice: The breath again. In the Gita, some offer the in-breath into the out-breath, one gift in a row of many. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sacrifice, offering. in Gita 4, breathing itself can be a yajna. some speakers say it closer to YUG-yuh.

carryVoice: Your line: even a breath can be yajna, an offering. One ordinary breath, set down as a gift. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.24 (the offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman)
Bhagavad Gita 4.25–4.28 (offerings of the senses, possessions, austerity, yoga, study)
Bhagavad Gita 4.29 (some offer prana into apana and apana into prana, restraining both)
Bhagavad Gita 5.27–5.28 (making prana and apana even within the nostrils; free of desire, fear and anger)
